subject: biology

items.q: Sodium chloride dissolves when it is placed in water. Which statement describes the attractions that hold the ions in solution?
items.correct: Na⁺ ions are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and Cl⁻ ions to the partially positive hydrogen atoms.
items.misconception: Hydrogen bonds form between each ion and the water molecules that surround it, just as they form between water molecules.
items.why: Hydrogen bonding is introduced as the explanation for nearly every property of water, so students reach for it to explain solvation of every solute. The guidance names both hydrogen bonds and attractions to ions, and the two are easily merged into one idea. Hydrogen bonds form between water molecules and polar molecules such as glucose, which have hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen. An ion has no such bond; it is held in solution by the attraction between its full charge and the partial charges on the polar water molecules around it.
items.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
items.random_wrong: Both kinds of ion are attracted to the oxygen end of the water molecules, because that is the end that carries a charge.

items.q: A student writes: "Glucose and sodium chloride both dissolve in water because water molecules form hydrogen bonds with them." How should this claim be evaluated?
items.correct: Correct for glucose, whose hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, but not for sodium chloride, whose ions are attracted to water's partial charges.
items.misconception: Incorrect for both: glucose dissociates into ions when it dissolves, and ions are held in solution by attraction to the partial charges on water, not by hydrogen bonds.
items.why: The first solvation example students meet is an ionic compound splitting into ions, so 'dissolving' and 'dissociating' become the same thing. Sugar solutions do not conduct electricity, but students rarely connect that fact with how sugar dissolves. Polar molecules dissolve without becoming ions. Glucose has several hydroxyl groups, each able to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, and this is enough to hold whole glucose molecules in solution. Only ionic compounds dissolve by separating into ions.
items.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules
items.random_wrong: Correct for both: hydrogen bonds are the attraction that holds every kind of dissolved particle in solution, whether it is a molecule or an ion.

items.q: Two sucrose solutions, 0.2 mol dm⁻³ and 0.6 mol dm⁻³, are separated by a membrane that is permeable to water but not to sucrose. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Water moves by osmosis from the hypotonic 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution into the hypertonic 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solution.
items.misconception: Water moves by osmosis from the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution into the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution, down the concentration gradient.
items.why: Osmosis is taught alongside diffusion, and the rule 'high concentration to low concentration' is remembered as a general rule. When the word 'concentrated' is then applied to a solution, students move the water in the direction the rule seems to demand, forgetting that the rule was about the solute. Osmosis is the net movement of water from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration. Express the direction in terms of solute concentration: water moves from the hypotonic solution into the hypertonic solution.
items.specStatementText: Osmosis: water moves towards the higher solute concentration
items.random_wrong: Water moves by osmosis from the 0.2 mol dm⁻³ solution, which is hypertonic, into the 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution, which is hypotonic.

items.q: The cytoplasm of a red blood cell has a solute concentration equivalent to 0.9% sodium chloride. A red blood cell is placed in a 3% sodium chloride solution. What is the net movement across its membrane, and what happens to the cell?
items.correct: Water moves out of the cell, because the solution is hypertonic to the cytoplasm, so the cell shrinks and becomes crenated.
items.misconception: Water moves into the cell and it swells, because the 3% solution is hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cell.
items.why: The prefixes hypo- and hyper- sound alike and are easily swapped, and the ending -tonic suggests strength, so students who remember that cells shrink in one of the two solutions attach the wrong prefix to it. Hypo- means below and hyper- means above, and both refer to solute concentration. A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the solution it is compared with; a hypertonic solution has a higher one; isotonic solutions have the same solute concentration. Water moves by osmosis from hypotonic to hypertonic.
items.specStatementText: Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
items.random_wrong: Water moves into the cell and it swells, because water moves from the more concentrated solution to the less concentrated cytoplasm.

items.q: A cell is placed in a solution that is isotonic with its cytoplasm. Which statement describes the movement of water across its membrane?
items.correct: Water molecules cross the membrane in both directions at equal rates, so there is a dynamic equilibrium with no net movement.
items.misconception: Water molecules stop crossing the membrane in either direction, because there is no concentration gradient to drive them.
items.why: Osmosis is described as 'net movement', but the word 'net' is easily dropped, leaving the idea that movement itself requires a gradient. Diagrams show arrows only when there is a gradient, so the absence of an arrow is read as the absence of movement. Individual water molecules move randomly through the membrane all the time, whatever the concentrations. When the solution is isotonic with the cytoplasm, molecules enter and leave the cell at the same rate: this is a dynamic equilibrium, not an absence of movement.
items.specStatementText: Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
items.random_wrong: Solute molecules cross the membrane in both directions, keeping the concentrations on the two sides of the membrane equal.

items.q: Potato cylinders were bathed for 24 hours in sucrose solutions and their mean percentage change in mass recorded: 0.0 mol dm⁻³, +8.0%; 0.2 mol dm⁻³, +2.5%; 0.4 mol dm⁻³, −3.0%; 0.6 mol dm⁻³, −8.5%; 0.8 mol dm⁻³, −12.0%. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
items.correct: The potato cells are isotonic with sucrose of about 0.3 mol dm⁻³, the concentration at which the change in mass would be zero.
items.misconception: The isotonic concentration is exactly 0.2 mol dm⁻³, because that is the tested concentration with the change in mass closest to zero.
items.why: Students treat the tested concentrations as the only possible answers, because those are the only values in the results table. They read a graph as a set of points rather than as a continuous relationship from which a value between the points can be read. The isotonic solute concentration is deduced from the data, not chosen from them: percentage change in mass is plotted against concentration and the isotonic concentration is where the line crosses zero. It normally lies between two tested concentrations, and it can be estimated by interpolation.
items.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
items.random_wrong: The 0.6 mol dm⁻³ solution was hypotonic to the potato cells, which is why the cylinders bathed in it lost mass.

items.q: Five potato cylinders were bathed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. Their percentage changes in mass had a mean of −3.0%, a standard deviation of 1.0% and a standard error of 0.45%. What does the standard error indicate?
items.correct: How close the sample mean of −3.0% is likely to be to the true mean; it would decrease if more cylinders were measured.
items.misconception: The average size of the mistakes made in weighing the cylinders, which would be zero if the balance had been used correctly.
items.why: In everyday language an error is a mistake, and students carry that meaning into statistics. 'Error bars' on a graph then look like a confession of sloppy technique rather than a description of sampling. Standard error describes the precision of a sample mean as an estimate of the true mean; it arises from natural variation between samples, not from mistakes. Even flawless measurements of varied tissue give a standard error above zero, and the only way to reduce it is to measure more repeats.
items.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
items.random_wrong: The spread of the five individual percentage changes around their mean, which is the same thing that the standard deviation shows.

items.q: Red blood cells are placed in distilled water. What happens to them, and why?
items.correct: Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell and burst, because no wall resists their expansion.
items.misconception: Water enters by osmosis and the cells swell until their membranes are stretched taut, and then they remain turgid.
items.why: Turgidity is the vivid outcome students remember from plant cells, and they assume the cell membrane can resist pressure in the same way as a cell wall. The membrane is drawn as a firm line, which looks strong. Only a cell wall can withstand the pressure that builds up as water enters. An animal cell has no wall, so in a hypotonic medium it swells and, if the difference in solute concentration is large enough, it bursts; in a hypertonic medium it shrinks and crenates.
items.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
items.random_wrong: Water leaves by osmosis, because the cytoplasm is more concentrated than the distilled water, and the cells shrink.

items.q: Paramecium is a unicellular organism that lives in fresh water. Its contractile vacuole repeatedly fills with water and then expels it from the cell. Why is this necessary?
items.correct: The cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, so water continually enters by osmosis and must be expelled to prevent swelling and bursting.
items.misconception: The vacuole stores the water the cell absorbs, keeping a reserve that the cell can draw on when the pond water becomes scarce.
items.why: The word 'vacuole' is associated with storage from the plant vacuole, and water is thought of as something a cell needs rather than something that can harm it. The vacuole is seen filling up, which looks like storage. A contractile vacuole is a device for removing water, not storing it. Water enters a freshwater cell continuously by osmosis; the vacuole collects this water and contracts to push it out of the cell, using energy, so that the cell does not swell and burst.
items.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
items.random_wrong: The vacuole takes in water to replace the water the cell loses by osmosis to the fresh water, which is more dilute than the cytoplasm.

items.q: Which statement about the tissue fluid that bathes the cells of a mammal is correct?
items.correct: It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they neither swell and burst nor shrink through net osmosis.
items.misconception: It is kept slightly hypotonic to the cytoplasm of the cells, so that they are kept fully hydrated by a steady inflow of water.
items.why: Health messages about drinking plenty of water lead students to think more water is always better for cells. They do not connect this with what they know happens to a wall-less cell in a hypotonic medium. Cells without walls are damaged by net water movement in either direction. Multicellular organisms therefore maintain isotonic tissue fluid, so that there is a dynamic equilibrium and no net gain or loss of water by the cells.
items.specStatementText: Cells without walls swell, burst, shrink or crenate
items.random_wrong: It is kept isotonic with the cytoplasm of the cells, so that no water molecules cross their membranes at all.

items.q: A strip of onion epidermis is mounted in a concentrated sucrose solution and viewed under a microscope. Which statement describes what happens to its cells?
items.correct: Water leaves each cell by osmosis, the protoplast shrinks and its membrane pulls away from the wall: the cells are plasmolysed.
items.misconception: Water leaves each cell by osmosis and the whole cell, wall included, shrinks and crumples inward, just as an animal cell crenates.
items.why: Students learn about crenation of animal cells and expect a plant cell to lose water in the same way. Diagrams of plasmolysis are often small, and the rigid wall staying put while the contents pull away is not noticed. The cellulose cell wall is rigid and freely permeable. When water leaves a plant cell in a hypertonic solution the protoplast shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the wall, but the wall keeps its shape: this is plasmolysis, and it is quite different from crenation.
items.specStatementText: Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
items.random_wrong: Water leaves each cell by osmosis and an empty space forms between the wall and the membrane, because the wall lets nothing through.

items.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. What happens to it?
items.correct: Water enters by osmosis and the cell becomes turgid, its wall resisting further expansion.
items.misconception: Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells until it bursts, like an animal cell in pure water.
items.why: Bursting is the dramatic outcome learned for red blood cells, and students transfer it to all cells. The role of the wall in resisting pressure is easy to overlook because the wall is described mainly as 'giving shape'. In a hypotonic medium water enters a plant cell by osmosis, but the cellulose wall resists expansion. Pressure builds up against the wall (turgor pressure) until it stops any further net entry of water. The cell becomes turgid and does not burst.
items.specStatementText: Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
items.random_wrong: Solutes leave the cell into the pure water until the cell sap is as dilute as the water outside.

items.q: A patient who has lost a large volume of blood is given fluid intravenously. Why is 0.9% sodium chloride solution chosen rather than pure water?
items.correct: It is isotonic with blood plasma, so the patient's blood cells neither take in water and burst nor lose water and crenate.
items.misconception: Pure water would be absorbed too slowly by the blood cells, whereas the sodium chloride solution enters them quickly.
items.why: Rehydration is thought of as 'adding water', and drinking pure water is harmless because the gut and kidneys adjust the concentration before it reaches the cells. Students do not realise that fluid put straight into the blood bypasses those controls. Intravenous fluids must be isotonic with blood plasma, for example 0.9% sodium chloride solution. Pure water injected into a vein would make the plasma hypotonic to the red blood cells, which would take in water and burst.
items.specStatementText: Isotonic solutions in medicine
items.random_wrong: The patient has lost salt along with the blood, and the purpose of the solution is to replace that salt in the plasma.

items.q: A kidney removed for transplantation is bathed in a solution while it is stored. Which type of solution is used, and why?
items.correct: An isotonic solution, so that the kidney's cells neither gain nor lose water by net osmosis while the organ is stored.
items.misconception: Sterile distilled water, so that the cells stay well hydrated and no solutes can enter the organ before it is transplanted.
items.why: Rehydration is thought of as 'adding water', and drinking pure water is harmless because the gut and kidneys adjust the concentration before it reaches the cells. Students do not realise that fluid put straight into the blood bypasses those controls. Intravenous fluids must be isotonic with blood plasma, for example 0.9% sodium chloride solution. Pure water injected into a vein would make the plasma hypotonic to the red blood cells, which would take in water and burst.
items.specStatementText: Isotonic solutions in medicine
items.random_wrong: A slightly hypotonic solution, so that the cells are kept fully hydrated by a steady inward flow of water.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes water potential and the scale on which it is measured?
items.correct: It is the potential energy of water per unit volume, measured in kPa relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, which is set at zero.
items.misconception: It is the absolute potential energy of water per unit volume, so pure water at 20°C has a value of zero because its molecules have no potential energy.
items.why: In most measurements zero means 'none', and students carry that over. They are not used to scales like the Celsius scale, where zero is simply a chosen reference and negative values are ordinary. It is impossible to measure the absolute quantity of the potential energy of water. Water potential is therefore measured relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, which is defined as zero; a negative value means less potential energy than that reference, not an absence of potential energy.
items.specStatementText: Water potential: energy per unit volume, measured against pure water
items.random_wrong: It is the potential energy of water per unit volume, which is zero for pure water and rises to positive values as more and more solute is dissolved in it.

items.q: Two adjacent plant cells have water potentials of −300 kPa (cell A) and −900 kPa (cell B). Which statement describes the net movement of water between them?
items.correct: From A to B, because water moves from higher to lower water potential and loses potential energy.
items.misconception: From B to A, because −900 kPa is the larger number, so the water in B has the greater potential energy.
items.why: Students compare the magnitudes of negative numbers and ignore the sign, especially when the numbers are given in a biology context rather than a mathematics one. The word 'higher' is also read as 'larger'. Water potential values are negative numbers on a scale whose top is zero. The value nearer to zero is the higher water potential and its water has more potential energy, so water moves from −300 kPa to −900 kPa, losing potential energy as it moves from higher to lower water potential.
items.specStatementText: Water moves from higher to lower water potential
items.random_wrong: There is no net movement, because both values are negative, so neither cell's water has any potential energy.

items.q: A plant cell has a solute potential of −700 kPa and a pressure potential of +200 kPa. What is its water potential?
items.correct: -500 kPa
items.misconception: -900 kPa
items.why: Students treat the equation as 'add up the numbers' and drop the signs, or they reason that turgor pressure is one more thing making the cell 'attract' water. Signed arithmetic is easy to get wrong when the units and symbols are unfamiliar. Solute potential is negative and pressure potential inside a cell is positive, so they partly cancel: ψw = ψs + ψp = −700 + 200 = −500 kPa. A positive pressure potential raises the water potential of a cell, making it less negative, which is why a turgid cell stops taking in water.
items.specStatementText: Solute and pressure potentials add up: ψw = ψs + ψp
items.random_wrong: -700 kPa

items.q: Which statement about the solute potential and pressure potential of water in plant structures is correct?
items.correct: Solute potential is zero for pure water and negative for any solution; pressure potential is usually positive in cells but negative in xylem sap under tension.
items.misconception: Pressure potential is positive throughout the plant, including in the xylem vessels, because a pressure lower than zero cannot exist in a liquid.
items.why: In everyday experience pressure is something that pushes, and students have met only positive pressures. The cell wall pushing inward is the first example of pressure potential they see, so they generalise it to all plant structures. Water in xylem vessels is pulled upward as a continuous column under tension, and tension is a negative pressure. The pressure potential of xylem sap is therefore negative, which is part of why its water potential is very low.
items.specStatementText: Solute and pressure potentials add up: ψw = ψs + ψp
items.random_wrong: Solute potential is positive in cell sap, because dissolving solutes adds potential energy to the water, and it is negative only in xylem sap.

items.q: Plant tissue is bathed in pure water. Which statement explains, in terms of solute and pressure potentials, why net uptake of water by its cells eventually stops?
items.correct: Water entering raises the pressure potential as the wall resists expansion, until it cancels the solute potential and the cell's water potential is zero.
items.misconception: Water enters until the cell wall has been stretched to its limit, and the fully stretched wall then physically prevents any more water from passing into the cell.
items.why: Students picture the wall as a container that is 'full', because a stretched balloon or bag stops accepting more. They do not see that water crosses the membrane on the basis of water potential, not of available space. Water enters and leaves in response to the water potential gradient. As water enters, the wall presses back with increasing pressure, raising the pressure potential. At full turgor ψp equals the magnitude of ψs, the cell's water potential is zero, equal to pure water, and there is a dynamic equilibrium: water still crosses the membrane, but with no net movement.
items.specStatementText: Explaining turgor and plasmolysis with potentials
items.random_wrong: Uptake does not stop: water keeps entering until the pressure potential exceeds what the wall can withstand and the cell bursts.

items.q: Plant tissue is bathed in a sucrose solution with a water potential of −2500 kPa. The cells initially have a solute potential of −900 kPa and a pressure potential of +600 kPa. Which statement explains what happens?
items.correct: Water leaves the cells; pressure potential falls to zero as the protoplast pulls away from the wall, so ψw equals ψs for each cell.
items.misconception: Water leaves the cells; pressure potential becomes negative as the shrinking protoplast pulls inward on the cell wall that surrounds it.
items.why: Students learn that negative pressure potentials exist in the xylem and apply the idea to any cell that is 'under strain'. Diagrams of plasmolysis showing the membrane stretched between corners of the wall suggest that it is being pulled. Once the protoplast has shrunk away from the wall, there is no wall pressure on the cell contents, so pressure potential is zero and the water potential of the cell equals its solute potential. Negative pressure potentials arise in xylem vessels, where a column of sap is under tension, not in plasmolysed cells.
items.specStatementText: Explaining turgor and plasmolysis with potentials
items.random_wrong: Water leaves the cells; the wall contracts with the protoplast, so the pressure potential stays positive as the cell shrinks.

items.q: Five potato cylinders were bathed in 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose for 24 hours. The mean percentage change in mass was −3.0% with a standard deviation of 1.0%; the mean percentage change in length was −2.0% with a standard deviation of 2.5%. What do these data indicate?
items.correct: The mass measurements were more reliable than the length measurements, because the mass repeats were less widely spread around their mean.
items.misconception: Every mass repeat lay within 1.0% of the mean and every length repeat within 2.5% of it, because the standard deviations give the range of each set.
items.why: Range bars and standard-error bars look identical on a graph, and range is the measure of spread students learn first, so they read every bar as a range. A standard-error bar extends one standard error above and below the mean. It indicates how precisely the mean has been estimated, not the limits of the data: individual repeats normally lie well outside it.
items.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
items.random_wrong: The length measurements contained more mistakes, because a larger standard deviation means that more errors were made when the ruler was used.

items.q: Which end of a water molecule is attracted to a negatively charged ion such as Cl⁻?
items.correct: The hydrogen atoms, which carry partial positive charges. Positively charged ions are attracted to the oxygen atom, which carries a partial negative charge.
items.misconception: Water molecules surround every ion with their oxygen atoms pointing inward, because the oxygen end is the charged end of the molecule.
items.why: Diagrams of a hydrated sodium ion, with oxygen atoms pointing inward, are far more common than diagrams of a hydrated chloride ion, so students generalise the picture. They also think of oxygen as 'the' charged atom and forget that the hydrogen atoms carry an equal and opposite partial charge. Water is polar: the oxygen atom is partially negative and the hydrogen atoms are partially positive. Positively charged ions are attracted to the oxygen end of water molecules; negatively charged ions are attracted to the hydrogen end. Both kinds of ion are hydrated, but the water molecules are oriented in opposite ways.
items.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules

items.q: Is dissolving sodium chloride in water a chemical reaction?
items.correct: No. The ions are separated from one another and surrounded by water molecules, but they remain Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions and no new substance is formed.
items.misconception: Water dissolves a solute by reacting with it and breaking it down into atoms or smaller particles.
items.why: In everyday language something that dissolves 'disappears', and students who learned that acids 'attack' or 'dissolve' metals carry the idea of a chemical change over to solvation. The separation of a crystal into invisible ions looks like the solute being destroyed. Solvation is a physical process. Water molecules are attracted to the ions or polar molecules of the solute, pull them apart from one another and surround them, but the particles themselves are unchanged: evaporating the water recovers the original solute.
items.specStatementText: How water dissolves ions and polar molecules

items.q: When a cell is placed in a solution of different solute concentration, what crosses the membrane to bring the two sides towards equilibrium?
items.correct: Water, by osmosis. The solutes that set up the difference generally cannot cross the membrane, which is why water moves instead.
items.misconception: The concentrations are equalised by solute diffusing across the membrane from the more concentrated side to the less concentrated side.
items.why: Students first learn diffusion of solutes and think of every concentration difference as something the solute itself removes. The fact that a membrane is partially permeable, letting water through but not many solutes, is stated once and easily forgotten. Osmosis happens precisely because the membrane is partially permeable: water can cross it but the solute cannot. The difference in solute concentration is reduced by water moving from the hypotonic side to the hypertonic side, which dilutes the more concentrated solution and concentrates the more dilute one.
items.specStatementText: Osmosis: water moves towards the higher solute concentration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How should the direction of osmosis be described?
items.correct: In terms of solute concentration: water moves from the solution with the lower solute concentration to the solution with the higher solute concentration, or from hypotonic to hypertonic.
items.misconception: Osmosis is water moving from a high concentration of water to a low concentration of water, so 'water concentration' is the quantity that decides which way water moves.
items.why: Earlier courses often teach osmosis as diffusion of water down its own concentration gradient, because it makes osmosis look like a special case of diffusion. The phrase is simple to remember and seems to give the right answer in dilute solutions. The IB guide requires the direction of movement to be expressed in terms of solute concentration, not water concentration, using the terms hypotonic, hypertonic and isotonic. 'Water concentration' is not a quantity that is measured, and at Higher Level it cannot account for the effect of pressure, which is why water potential is used instead.
items.specStatementText: Osmosis: water moves towards the higher solute concentration
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a cell have to use energy to move water across its membrane by osmosis?
items.correct: No. Osmosis is passive: water moves down the gradient by itself, and a cell cannot pump water directly to decide the direction.
items.misconception: The cell controls osmosis actively, pumping water in when it needs more and out when it has too much, and switching the pumping off in an isotonic solution.
items.why: Students learn that the cell membrane 'controls what enters and leaves the cell' and that some transport is active, and they extend this control to water. The contractile vacuole, which does use energy to remove water, reinforces the idea that the cell decides where water goes. Osmosis is a passive process that needs no energy from the cell: water moves from the hypotonic side to the hypertonic side of a membrane whether the cell 'wants' it or not. A cell can only influence osmosis indirectly, for example by changing its solute concentration or by expelling water that has already entered.
items.specStatementText: Predicting the direction of water movement for a cell
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do standard deviation and standard error describe the same thing?
items.correct: No. Standard deviation describes the spread of the individual measurements around their mean; standard error describes how close the sample mean is likely to be to the true mean.
items.misconception: Standard error is simply another name for standard deviation, and both describe how spread out the individual measurements are.
items.why: The two statistics have similar names, are calculated from the same data and are met in the same lesson. Because standard error is derived from standard deviation, students assume it carries the same meaning. Standard deviation is a property of the data: it describes the spread of the repeats and is used to compare the reliability of length and mass measurements. Standard error is a property of the mean: it is smaller than the standard deviation, decreases as the number of repeats rises, and can be shown graphically as error bars.
items.specStatementText: Finding a tissue's isotonic concentration, and judging the data
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What fills the gap between the cell wall and the cell membrane in a plasmolysed cell?
items.correct: The external solution, which passes freely through the cell wall.
items.misconception: The gap is empty, because the cell wall is a barrier that stops the outside solution getting in.
items.why: Students see the wall as the cell's outer barrier and assume it is impermeable like the membrane. In diagrams the gap is drawn as white space, which looks empty. The cell wall is freely permeable to water and dissolved solutes; only the cell membrane is partially permeable. As the protoplast shrinks away from the wall, the hypertonic external solution flows through the wall and fills the space.
items.specStatementText: Cells with walls become turgid or plasmolyse
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does an intravenous drip contain sodium chloride?
items.correct: To make the solution isotonic with blood plasma, so that the patient's cells neither gain nor lose water by net osmosis.
items.misconception: The sodium chloride is there because the patient is short of salt, and the purpose of the drip is to replace it.
items.why: Students look for a nutritional reason for each ingredient. 'Saline' sounds like a salt supplement, and sports drinks are marketed as replacing lost salts. The concentration of a saline drip (0.9% sodium chloride) is chosen so that it is isotonic with blood plasma. Its purpose is osmotic: to add fluid to the blood without changing its solute concentration, so that no harmful net movement of water into or out of cells occurs.
items.specStatementText: Isotonic solutions in medicine
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does dissolving solute in water raise or lower its water potential?
items.correct: It lowers it. Pure water has a water potential of zero, and every solution at atmospheric pressure has a negative water potential.
items.misconception: Adding solute raises the water potential to a positive value, because a solution has more in it than pure water.
items.why: 'More concentrated' sounds like 'more', and students expect a bigger quantity to give a bigger number. They have also learned that solutions attract water, and 'attracting' feels like a positive property. Water potential is highest in pure water, which is assigned the value zero. Solutes reduce the free energy of the water, so solute potential ranges from zero downwards and every solution has a negative water potential; the more concentrated the solution, the more negative its water potential.
items.specStatementText: Water potential: energy per unit volume, measured against pure water

items.q: Is the water potential of a plant cell determined only by the solute concentration of its sap?
items.correct: No. It is the sum of the solute potential and the pressure potential: ψw = ψs + ψp.
items.misconception: Only the solute concentration matters, so the water potential of a cell is equal to its solute potential and pressure has no effect.
items.why: At Standard Level osmosis is explained entirely in terms of solute concentration, and students keep that model when they move to water potential. Pressure is invisible in a microscope image, so it is not seen as part of the cell's condition. For a cell with a wall, the pressure exerted by the wall on the contents raises the water potential: ψw = ψs + ψp. Two cells with identical sap can have different water potentials if their pressure potentials differ, and it is this that explains why a turgid cell in pure water stops taking in water while its sap is still concentrated.
items.specStatementText: Solute and pressure potentials add up: ψw = ψs + ψp
